data.title: Altération doctrinale de la “Lettre à Epictète” de Saint Athanase
data.abstractNote: "Le problème historique, celui de l'existence, vers 433, de deux formes, l'une pure et l'autre corrompue, du texte de la lettre à Epictète, nous paraît résolu avec certitude par la réponse affirmative et en faveur de la sincérité du témoignage de saint Cyrille. Le problème critique, celui de l'identification et du discernement de ces deux formes, nous paraît également recevoir une solution certaine par l'affirmation de l'authenticité de la forme généralement transmise et reçue et de l'altération de la forme conservée par la version syriaque. Pour rester, à la rigueur, une hypothèse, l'attribution de la corruption du document aux Apollinaristes modérés n'en jouit pas moins, à nos yeux, de la plus grande probabilité de vérité. Quoi qu'il en soit d'ailleurs de ce dernier point, il reste que nous connaissons désormais, dans la littérature athanasienne authentique. un écrit conservé dans deux formes et dont le texte corrompu se recontre dans la forme qui semble la plus favorable à la christologie dite alexandrine. La tradition manuscrite et littéraire semble attester que la pluralité des formes n'est pas, parmi les ouvrages du grand Alexandrin, l'apanage exclusif de la lettre à Epictète." (pp. 760-761)

data.title: The Preservation of the Hexaplaric Materials in the Syrohexapla of III Kingdoms
data.abstractNote: The Syrohexapla (Syh) is widely believed to be a faithful witness to the Hexapla of Origen. This Syriac version was produced in the seventh century on the basis of Greek texts related to Origen's six-columned masterpiece of biblical scholarship. In Syh are preserved the signs used by Origen in the Hexapla to mark the divergences between the Greek and Hebrew texts, and also the readings of several Greek Jewish versions which are no longer fully extant. This thesis evaluates Syh as a witness to these hexaplaric materials in III Kingdoms (I Kings). Each of the nearly 600 signs preserved in Syh is analysed. They are divided among correctly marked asterisks, correctly marked obeli, and inaccurately marked readings. The 333 readings attributed to the Greek Jewish versions are treated separately. Finally, by including a chapter which examines a portion of the many readings in Syh for which no hexaplaric sign has been preserved, we are able to balance our sanguinity when considering the reliability of Syh for studying the remains of Origen's Hexapla. The number of materials preserved in our version compared with the number preserved in other witnesses is striking. In this study, we discover that no other witness compares to Syh as a trident of the hexaplaric tradition. However, the Conclusion argues that the textual scholar must use Syh with a cautious optimism: while our version is the best witness to the hexaplaric tradition that we possess, it is by no means a flawless one. This thesis prepares the way for a new critical edition of the hexaplaric fragments of III Kingdoms, which is now possible due to the results of the present study. Ultimately, this material will allow us to learn more about the interactions between Jews and Christians in the Graeco-Roman and Late Antique periods, their understandings of the nature of Scripture, and the methods they used to make the Divine Word understandable.

data.title: Eine übersehene Textvariante in den Oden Salomos (OdSal 36,1a)
data.abstractNote: In one of the two Syriac manuscripts of the Odes of Solomon, the first line of Ode 36 reads clearly as follows: “I rested on/upon the Spirit of the Lord” (Codex Nitriensis [N], MS. Add. 14538, British Museum). Since 1909 the same reading has been assumed for the other manuscript (Codex Harris [H], Cod. Syr. 9, John Rylands Library). However, it has been overlooked that this particular manuscript also reveals a slight correction, turning the meaning of this verse upside down. Moreover, this varia lectio probably reflects the original Greek reading and gives this verse a christological perspective: “The Spirit of the Lord rested on/upon me” (cf. Isaiah 11:2 and 61:1).

data.title: Naṣr Allâh Šalaq al-‘Âqûrí (Vittorio Scialac Accurense) e il suo ruolo politico e culturale tra Roma, Firenze e Ravenna
data.abstractNote: Vittorio Scialac Accurensis was among the first students who left his homeland in Lebanon to attempt his cultural and theological formation in the Maronite college founded by Pope Gregory XIII in 1584 in Rome. After completing his studies, he chose to remain in Italy, where he could get in touch with some influential personalities of his time, such as the Drusus prince Faḫr al-Dín II al-Ma‘ní and Cosimo II Medici. In this article both Scialac’s contributions to the cultural life of the beginning of 17th century Rome and his political-diplomatic activism will be analysed. Eventually, an unpublished letter addressed to Cosimo II is published in which the Maronite priest asks for the direction of the Medici printing house, which after the death of G. B. Raimondi in 1614 had fallen into a state of neglect.

data.title: Note sur la datation conservée en syriaque du Concile de Gangres
data.abstractNote: "La contradiction entre la date consulaire et l'ère d'Antioche transmises par la version syriaque des canons du concile de Gangres ne démontre pas que ces données sont dépourvues d'authenticité. La contradiction peut être attribuée à la négligence d'un copiste. Une telle négligence n'a pas pu concerner la datation consulaire. La datation à 343, selon le consulat de Placidus et Romulus, est donc à retenir comme correcte. Elle est également à préférer à la seule indication contraire fournie par les sources littéraires: l'affirmation de Socrate selon laquelle ce concile a eu lieu après le concile de Constantinople."
